questions.explanation: A parent job is not complete until all its children complete, even after its own body has finished. So `job.join()` waits for the inner `launch`, and "joined" comes last.

questions.question: Which statement best describes what structured concurrency guarantees?
options: Each coroutine lives in a scope that waits for its children and gets their failures
Coroutines in the same scope always run sequentially in the order they were launched
Coroutines launched in a scope always run on the same thread as the scope's creator
A coroutine that throws is silently restarted by its parent scope
questions.explanation: Structured concurrency ties a coroutine's lifetime to its scope: no coroutine is leaked, the parent waits for its children, and errors are not lost because they propagate up. It says nothing about ordering or threads, and nothing is retried automatically.

questions.question: Which of these are `CoroutineContext` elements that can be combined with `+`? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: `Job`, `CoroutineDispatcher` and `CoroutineName` all implement `CoroutineContext.Element`. `CoroutineStart.LAZY` is a separate `start` parameter of `launch`/`async`, and a `CoroutineScope` is not an element. It only wraps a context.

questions.question: A coroutine launched with `scope.launch { }` has started three child coroutines with `launch`, and all of them are suspended in `delay`. What happens when you call `cancel()` on the parent job?
options: The parent and all three children are cancelled
Only the parent is cancelled, and the children keep running until they finish
The parent waits for the children to finish normally and then cancels itself
Nothing happens until the children call `cancel()` themselves
questions.explanation: Cancellation flows down the Job hierarchy: cancelling a parent cancels every child (and their children). That is why cancelling a scope in `onCleared`/`onDestroy` stops all the work started from it.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: A child inherits its parent's context, so the first `launch` sees "root". In `a + b`, both elements have the same key `CoroutineName`, so the right-hand one replaces the left, and the element passed to `launch` overrides the inherited one.

questions.question: Calling `cancel()` on a child job also cancels its parent and its siblings.
questions.explanation: False. Cancelling a child (a `CancellationException`) is treated as normal and is not propagated up, so the parent and siblings keep running. Only a failure with a real exception cancels the parent in a regular Job hierarchy.

questions.question: A repository creates `val scope = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO)` without passing any `Job`. What happens?
options: `CoroutineScope()` adds a `Job()` automatically, so `scope.cancel()` cancels its coroutines
The scope has no Job, so `scope.cancel()` throws `IllegalStateException`
Each `launch` in this scope becomes a top-level coroutine that can't be cancelled through the scope
The scope uses a `SupervisorJob()` by default
questions.explanation: `CoroutineScope(context)` adds a plain `Job()` when the context has none, so the scope can be cancelled and acts as the parent of its coroutines. It is a regular `Job`, not a `SupervisorJob`. Among the scope factories, `MainScope()` is the one that uses a `SupervisorJob()`.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `coroutineScope` suspends until its body and all its children complete. "C" prints first, then B (10 ms), then A (50 ms), and only after that does `work()` return so "D" prints.

questions.question: A custom view presenter has `private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main)` and starts a polling loop in it, but never calls `scope.cancel()`. The user leaves the screen. What happens?
options: The loop keeps running and holds the view, leaking it until the process dies
The loop stops automatically because `Dispatchers.Main` is tied to the Activity lifecycle
The `SupervisorJob` cancels the loop when the view is detached
The loop is garbage-collected together with the presenter as soon as the screen closes
questions.explanation: A hand-made scope knows nothing about lifecycles. Neither `Dispatchers.Main` nor `SupervisorJob` cancels anything on its own, and a running coroutine is reachable from the dispatcher, so it isn't collected. Call `scope.cancel()` in `onDestroy`/`onCleared` (or the presenter's detach) to end the work.

questions.question: In a ViewModel, `viewModelScope.launch(Dispatchers.Default) { ... }` is still a child of `viewModelScope` and is cancelled when the ViewModel is cleared.
questions.explanation: True. The context you pass is merged with the scope's context. Only the dispatcher is replaced, and the scope's Job is still the parent. Only passing a `Job` (such as `Job()` or `SupervisorJob()`) replaces the parent and breaks the link.

questions.question: `parent` launched two coroutines, and each of them launched one more coroutine. All are still running. What does `parent.children.count()` return?
options: 0, because `children` is filled in only once the jobs complete
1, because `children` returns the most recent child only
questions.explanation: `Job.children` is a `Sequence<Job>` of the job's direct children. Grandchildren are children of those children, so you'd have to walk the tree to reach them.

questions.question: What does this print to stdout? (Assume any uncaught exception only goes to stderr.)
questions.explanation: In `supervisorScope` a failing child does not cancel its siblings or the scope, so the second child still prints. The scope still waits for all its children, so "after scope" comes last.

questions.question: Inside `coroutineScope { }`, one child `launch` throws an `IOException` while two siblings are still running. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: The `coroutineScope` call rethrows the `IOException` to its caller
The scope waits for the cancelled siblings to finish before it rethrows
The siblings keep running and the exception is reported only after they finish
The `coroutineScope` call returns normally because the child failed, not the scope
questions.explanation: In a regular Job hierarchy a failing child cancels its parent, which cancels the other children. The scope completes only after all children have finished (including their cancellation), and then `coroutineScope` rethrows the original exception.

questions.question: Why is `viewModelScope` built on a `SupervisorJob` rather than a plain `Job`?
options: So that one failed child doesn't cancel the scope and all the other jobs in it
So that coroutines survive `onCleared()` and keep running after the ViewModel is destroyed
So that exceptions thrown in child coroutines are swallowed and never crash the app
So that coroutines run on `Dispatchers.Main` by default
questions.explanation: With a plain `Job`, one failing `launch` would cancel the scope, and every later `launch` in that ViewModel would be cancelled immediately. A `SupervisorJob` isolates failures between children, but an uncaught exception still reaches the exception handler and can crash the app. The Main dispatcher comes from a separate element.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: The failing child cancels the `coroutineScope`, which cancels the sibling before its `delay` ends, so "sibling done" never prints. `coroutineScope` then rethrows the exception, and the surrounding `try/catch` catches it.

questions.question: Inside `supervisorScope`, a child does `launch { launch { throw Exception() }; launch { delay(1000) } }`. Because of the supervisor, the failing grandchild does not cancel its sibling.
questions.explanation: False. Only the direct children of a supervisor are supervised. The grandchildren's parent is a regular child Job, so the failure cancels that child and its other children. The supervisor only stops the failure from going any higher.

questions.question: `scope` is a normal `CoroutineScope` with a Job. Which of these coroutines are NOT cancelled when `scope.cancel()` is called? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Passing a `Job()` or `SupervisorJob()` to `launch` makes that new job the coroutine's parent, so it is no longer a child of `scope`. `GlobalScope` has no Job at all. A dispatcher or a name only replaces that element, and the scope's Job stays the parent.

questions.question: A developer wants the two inner coroutines to fail independently. What does this print to stdout? (Assume any uncaught exception only goes to stderr.)
questions.explanation: The `SupervisorJob()` becomes the parent of the outer `launch`, but the inner coroutines are children of that outer coroutine's own regular Job. So the failure cancels the outer coroutine and "B done" never prints. The usual fix is `supervisorScope { }` or a scope that is built on a `SupervisorJob`.

questions.question: A screen-level helper calls `scope.cancel()` in `onStop()` and then `scope.launch { refresh() }` again in `onStart()`. What happens when the user comes back to the screen?
options: `refresh()` never runs again, because a cancelled scope stays cancelled
`refresh()` runs normally, because `launch` reactivates the scope's Job
`scope.launch` throws `IllegalStateException` because the scope is cancelled
questions.explanation: A cancelled Job is final. Coroutines launched into it are cancelled right away, and no error is reported, so the bug fails silently. To pause and resume work, use `scope.coroutineContext.cancelChildren()` or create a new scope for each start.
